prompt: Why does "the database is fragile" tend to lose against a sales request, by the lesson?
hint: What arrives with the sales request?

choices.text: An adjective cannot be weighed against reais
choices.why: Right: it loses on the comparison, not on the merits.

choices.text: Directors care more about sales than about engineering
choices.why: The lesson says the director is not short-sighted; the problem is the form of the claim.

choices.text: Engineers present it too late in the meeting
choices.why: Timing is not the reason the lesson gives.

choices.text: The claim is false, since databases are designed to cope with load
choices.why: None of the engineer's sentences in the table is false.

prompt: Match what the engineer says to what the director hears, by the lesson's table.
hint: Each describes the system; the director decides about the business.

pairs.right: engineering wants a quarter without features
a metaphor, so probably an exaggeration

pairs.right: a project with no end and no measurable result

prompt: Which statement of Knight Capital's risk would have been on the rung where the decision lived?

choices.text: A deploy mistake could cost more than the company is worth
choices.why: Right: that is the sentence that gets a budget.

choices.text: Deployments are manual, with no check across servers
choices.why: Also true and also a description of the system.

choices.text: The repurposed flag is a code smell
choices.why: Jargon on the bottom rung.

choices.text: Dead code is still deployed on the routing servers, and nobody owns it
choices.why: True, and on the bottom rung: the kind of sentence that sits in a backlog.

prompt: A risk happens twice a year and costs R$ 50,000 each time. What is its expected loss per year?
hint: Times per year, times cost each time.

prompt: What is the difference between the chronic loss and the tail risk in Marola's Friday problem?

choices.text: The chronic loss is larger every year
choices.why: Size is not the distinction the lesson draws.

choices.text: They are the same risk measured over different periods
choices.why: They have different causes and very different impacts per event.

choices.text: One is measured, the other's likelihood is judged
choices.why: Right: so one is stated with its source, the other with its reasoning.

choices.text: Only the tail risk costs money; the chronic one costs reputation
choices.why: The chronic loss is lost revenue every Friday.

prompt: What does the lesson say a risk matrix is good for?
hint: And what it cannot say on its own.

choices.text: Deciding which risks to accept automatically, by colour
choices.why: Acceptance is a decision by a named person.

choices.text: Putting a technical risk beside the business ones
choices.why: Right: on the picture the board already looks at, where it can be compared.

choices.text: Replacing the arithmetic, which directors do not read
choices.why: The lesson says the opposite: a square invites "why is it red?", and the arithmetic answers.

choices.text: Ranking risks precisely by expected loss
choices.why: Its bands are coarse; two risks a hundred times apart can share a square.

prompt: Boa Praça's contract renews in September. How should the effect of a Friday outage on that renewal appear in a risk document?
hint: Not every impact converts into reais.

choices.text: As a red square in the matrix with no explanation needed
choices.why: A square without reasoning invites exactly the question it cannot answer.

choices.text: In words, set beside the numbers, not turned into a figure
choices.why: Right: a precise figure for an unpriceable impact is false precision.

choices.text: It should be left out, since only money is comparable
choices.why: The lesson says it belongs in the list.

choices.text: As a figure, the annual contract value times the chance of losing it
choices.why: Nobody can estimate that chance honestly, and an invented number makes the real ones doubted.

prompt: 180 checkouts fail on a Friday and 40% of those customers do not come back successfully. How many orders are lost?
With 72 orders lost and an average basket of R$ 150, how much revenue is lost per Friday?
Marola loses R$ 561,600 of revenue a year and its gross margin is about 25%. About how much margin is lost a year?
Why was the 40% the number that most needed measuring rather than assuming?
hint: What did the first draft assume?

choices.text: Because the order logs were missing for those Fridays
choices.why: The logs existed; the question was what failed customers did next.

choices.text: It was the most likely to be challenged, and assuming 100% overstated the loss
choices.why: Right: the honest, smaller number is what made the rest believable.

choices.text: Because finance asked for it in a template
choices.why: Nobody required it; it was the most challengeable number.

choices.text: Because it made the loss look larger
choices.why: Measuring it made the loss two and a half times smaller.

prompt: When is accepting a risk a correct decision, by the lesson?

choices.text: When the engineers are too busy to deal with it
choices.why: That is accepting by default, which the lesson calls illegitimate.

choices.text: When reducing it costs more than it saves
choices.why: Right: decided by whoever owns the budget, and written down with a review date and a trigger.

choices.text: Never; every known risk must be reduced
choices.why: The lesson calls acceptance legitimate and the one engineers forget.

choices.text: When it is in a green square of the matrix
choices.why: A colour does not decide; a person with the budget does.

prompt: An accepted risk goes into the register with which of these? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: When it will be looked at again
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: A promise that it will not happen before the review
choices.why: Nobody can promise that; it is why the trigger exists.

choices.text: What would trigger an earlier look
choices.why: Yes: on 6 March, the trigger fired.

choices.text: Who accepted it
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: An engineer escalates every risk as critical. What does the lesson say happens?

choices.text: The risks all get fixed sooner
choices.why: Directors cannot fund everything at once; they start discounting instead.

choices.text: Directors learn to discount all of them, including the real one
choices.why: Right: reserve the alarm for the risk whose expected loss justifies it.

choices.text: The engineer is promoted for vigilance
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson suggests it.

choices.text: The board takes over risk management from the engineering team entirely
choices.why: A dramatic outcome the lesson does not describe.

prompt: Why is "two to four times a year" better than "three times a year" for the tail risk?
hint: Three reasons in the lesson; pick the one listed.

choices.text: It is easier to calculate
choices.why: It is no easier; it is more honest.

choices.text: It hides the estimate so it cannot be checked
choices.why: A range comes with its reasoning, which is there to be checked.

choices.text: It shows the uncertainty
choices.why: Right: and it invites "what would put us at the high end?" and survives being wrong.

choices.text: Directors prefer larger-sounding numbers on paper
choices.why: Not the reason, and a cynical one.

prompt: When is "pay a small amount to reduce the uncertainty before deciding" an honest option?
hint: Otherwise it is delay with a spreadsheet.

choices.text: Always, since more data is better
choices.why: Measuring something whose answer changes nothing is delay.

choices.text: When the answer would change the decision
choices.why: Right: April versus June, in Lívia's example.

choices.text: When the measurement costs nothing at all
choices.why: Cheap helps; the test is whether the answer matters.

choices.text: When the decider is reluctant to spend money
choices.why: Reluctance does not make the information useful.

prompt: Match each word to the range in Marola's version of Kent's scale.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

prompt: Lívia's table lists "two to four full stops a year" among the measurements, unlabelled. What does the lesson predict?

choices.text: A reader who spots it treats every number as a judgement
choices.why: Right: mixing the two without labels is how a careful estimate gets dismissed.

choices.text: The board approves faster, because it looks measured
choices.why: Maybe once, until somebody asks where it came from.

choices.text: Nothing, since the range already shows the uncertainty well enough
choices.why: A range shows width, not whether the number was measured.

choices.text: Finance recalculates it with its own assumptions
choices.why: Not the consequence the lesson names.
